content.why_desc: Linux file permissions are expressed in two formats — symbolic (rwxr-xr-x) and octal (755). Calculating the correct permission value manually is error-prone, especially with less common permission sets. Our calculator lets you click checkboxes to set permissions visually, and instantly generates both the octal value and the ready-to-use chmod command.

web.title: Web Server Files
web.desc: Set 644 for HTML/CSS/JS files (owner read/write, group/others read-only) on Apache or Nginx

scripts.title: Executable Scripts
scripts.desc: Set 755 for shell scripts (owner full, group/others read+execute) to make them runnable

ssh.title: SSH Key Files
ssh.desc: SSH requires private keys to be 600 (owner read/write only) or SSH will refuse to use them

uploads.title: Upload Directories
uploads.desc: Set 775 for web upload directories so the web server process can write user-uploaded files

never777.title: ✓ Never Use 777 in Production
never777.desc: chmod 777 gives everyone full read/write/execute access — a serious security risk. Use the minimum permissions necessary.

least.title: ✓ Principle of Least Privilege
least.desc: Always grant the minimum permissions needed. Start restrictive (600) and add permissions as needed rather than starting open.

recursive.title: ✓ Be Careful with -R Recursion
recursive.desc: chmod -R applies permissions recursively to all files and directories. Setting execute on directories is usually correct, but not always for files.

umask.title: ✓ Understand umask
umask.desc: The umask value subtracts permissions from the default. A umask of 022 means new files get 644 and new directories get 755 by default.

faq.a1: 755 means: Owner (7) = read+write+execute, Group (5) = read+execute, Others (5) = read+execute. It's the standard permission for executable files and public directories.
faq.q2: What is the difference between 644 and 755?
faq.a2: 644 (rw-r--r--): Owner can read/write, others can only read — used for regular files. 755 (rwxr-xr-x): Owner can also execute — used for scripts and directories.
faq.q3: Why does my SSH key need 600 permissions?
faq.a3: SSH refuses to use private keys that are accessible by any other user. The 600 permission (rw-------) ensures only the owner can read/write the key, preventing unauthorized access.
faq.q4: What does the execute bit on a directory mean?
faq.a4: For directories, the execute bit means 'traverse' — it allows users to enter the directory and access files within it. Without execute permission on a directory, users cannot cd into it even if they have read permission.
